linguisticReconstructions.claim: The jamu is a patrilineal clan name: it designates membership in a descent group, not an individual filiation to the father.

The clan name Jàra, of which Diarra is the usual French transcription, is identical to the Bambara word jàra, which means the lion (wáraba is its synonym) and, in a second sense that the dictionary gives separately, the fetish. No source consulted says whether the clan takes its name from the beast, from the fetish or from something else: the origin of the name is not established.

The Jàra entry of the dictionary of jamuw reports a prohibition specific to the clan: a Jàra must not look at a newborn child during the first eight days after its birth, otherwise the child would die. This note is carried only by that entry and is not corroborated by any other source consulted.

sources.title: EthniAfrica — fiche du peuple Bambara, organisation clanique
sources.notes: Taken from the "Clan organisation" chapter of the Bambara people's fiche.

sources.title: Beyond the Mali Empire — A New Paradigm for the Sunjata Epic
sources.notes: Jansen, Jan, Universiteit Leiden. Critical work on the transmission of the epic and on the jamu as a social institution rather than as historical memory; used here for the nature of the jamu, not to date an ancestor.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Onomastic annex of the Bamadaba, the electronic Bambara-French dictionary supplementing the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA); the annex of clan names is identified as such by Vydrin, « Vers une lexicographie mandingue sur la base de grands corpus annotés », Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. 375 entries in MDF format, consulted in the complete file. The file provides no legend for its markers, and the reading adopted is the one the file imposes: \ca carries the Mandinka status terms themselves (nùmu, jèli, hɔ́rɔn, garanke, finɛ, tontigi, wage, gesere); \sn is read as senankun because the Kúyate entry annotates its own line « \sn Keyita » with a reservation stating that this relation is a friendly understanding and not a senankuya. The \sn links are not systematically reciprocal from one entry to another: each pair is therefore cited according to the entry that carries it, named in the claim or the gap. The Jàra entry carries the group markers b (Bambara) and m, read as a Malinke indication by cross-checking with the Kéyità entry, which another of our fiches documents as a Malinke jamu; its \sn links name Tarawele, Denbele, Sanogo, Kone, Kanute, Dunbuya and Bagayogo, and the note on newborns is written there in Russian, translated here.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, number 38, 2002, p. 175-197. Field survey in Mali. She sets out what the pact obliges: the relation holds in perpetuity for the entire descent of both lineages, marriage between them is prohibited — variably applied today, she notes — and mutual aid is owed without reserve. Cited for the obligation itself; she does not name the pair on this fiche, which is carried by the entries cited alongside her.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, number 184, 2006, p. 687 and following. Cited for the caution it raises: the idea that joking kinship would ease conflicts is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, hence as a discourse to be analysed rather than a measured effect. The starting page is verified, the ending page is not.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire bambara-français, lexique
sources.notes: Online version of the electronic Bambara-French dictionary whose annex of clan names is cited separately. The article jàra is glossed there « lion, Panthera leo », with wáraba as a synonym, then « fetish »; a second article Jàra lists it among the clan names. Consulted online on 29 September 2026.

gaps.reason: The jamu appears neither among the numu lineages nor among the jeli lineages that Charry lists; nor does it appear in the short list of jamuw horon that he gives (Keita, Konaté, Koné, Traoré). The jamuw dictionary, which assigns a status to seven of the ten Mande jamuw in the set, carries none for the Jàra entry. The horon status that current directories attribute to the name therefore remains unfound in a dedicated source, and is not asserted here.

The General History of Africa documents Ngolo Diarra (1766-1790) and the Ngolosi dynasty that succeeded him at length, but presents him as a ton-jon who rose to power: it does not at any point link his jamu to the Bamana Jara clan. The link would be a patronymic homonymy, which this field excludes, and not a descent. No other bearer has been linked to the clan.

Diarra and Jara are two spellings of the same jamu. The jamuw dictionary lists Condé, Ndiaye and Koné among the equivalences of the Jàra entry — clan names of other peoples held to be the same, not homonyms. No distinct lineage of origin has been found, but since the etymology of the name itself remains open, a homonymy could not be ruled out on this basis.
